issues.title: [MPS] Tracking issue: sparse compressed (CSR/CSC/BSR/BSC) tensor support
issues.body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

Tracking issue for bringing sparse compressed tensors (CSR, CSC, BSR, BSC) to the
MPS backend, and for the MPS defects found while doing it.

**Motivation.** `torch.sparse_csr_tensor(..., device="mps")` currently fails with
`Could not run 'new_compressed_tensor' from the 'mps:0' device`, which is
#129842 (closed as completed while the reproducer in its body still fails) and
#166426 (closed as a duplicate of it).

Concretely, scvi-tools loads single-cell count matrices as CSR and offers
`load_sparse_tensor=True`, whose purpose is to move the compressed representation
to the accelerator and densify only after the transfer, in
`on_after_batch_transfer`. Because the transfer fails on MPS the library probes
for support and densifies on the host instead, sending a dense count matrix over
the bus where the data is typically more than 90% zeros. That is the exact cost
the option exists to avoid.

**State of the backend.** Most of the plumbing already exists: `SparseCsrMPS` is
generated from the MPS backend component and the `SparseCsr` functionality key,
and `Backend.h`, `Layout.h` and `DispatchKey.cpp` handle it. What was missing was
the constructor case, the key-set/device invariant in `SparseCsrTensorImpl`, and
a hard-coded device allowlist in `_validate_sparse_compressed_tensor_args`.

### Plan

A stack of four changes, the first three independent of the sparse work and
useful on their own:

1. **Metal shader header dependencies.** On a host where `CAN_COMPILE_METAL` is
   `NO`, the embedded shader sources are not regenerated when a header under
   `c10/metal/` changes, so an edit silently does not reach the binary.
2. **GPU hang in `scatter_reduce`/`index_reduce` with NaN.** The CAS loop behind
   `amax`/`amin`/`prod` compares floats, so once a NaN is stored the exchange
   never succeeds and the loop spins forever. Separately, `index_reduce_`
   `amin`/`amax` dropped NaN where CPU propagates it.
3. **`binary_cross_entropy` on zero-element tensors**, which trips
   `Placeholder tensor is empty!` for want of a `numel() == 0` guard.
4. **Sparse compressed tensors on MPS**: construction, transfer, the layout
   conversions, the device-agnostic structural and elementwise operations, and
   two Metal kernels for `_convert_indices_from_coo_to_csr` and
   `_convert_indices_from_csr_to_coo`, which every layout conversion is built on.

### Not covered by the first stack

These need real Metal kernels rather than dispatch registrations, because their
`.out` variants resolve to `sparse::impl::cpu::add_out_sparse_csr` or to cuSPARSE
and MKL, so there is no shared implementation to reuse:

- [ ] `addmm`, `mm` (SpMM)
- [ ] `addmv` (SpMV)
- [ ] `add` (sparse + sparse)
- [ ] `sampled_addmm`
- [ ] `sum` and `prod` over a dimension (`_sparse_csr_sum`, `_sparse_csr_prod`)
- [ ] `bmm`, `baddbmm`
- [ ] `_sparse_mm_reduce_impl`
- [ ] `triangular_solve`
- [ ] `segment_reduce`, which `torch.masked` reductions over a compressed tensor
      need and which has no MPS kernel either

### Known issues

- #196190: `mul` on an integer CSR tensor intermittently produces an invalid
  compressed tensor.

This issue was authored with the help of an AI assistant (Claude).


cc @nikitaved @pearu @cpuhrsch @amjames @bhosmer @jcaip @kulinseth @malfet @DenisVieriu97 @jhavukainen @aditvenk @Isalia20

issues.title: General MPS op coverage tracking issue
issues.body:
### This issue is to have a centralized place to list and track work on adding support to new ops for the MPS backend.

[**Most requested ops**](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/154052) (extracted from comments to this issue and #141287)

[**PyTorch MPS Ops Project**](https://github.com/users/kulinseth/projects/1/views/1) : Project to track all the ops for MPS backend. There are a very large number of operators in pytorch and so they are not all yet implemented. We will be prioritizing adding new operators based on user feedback. If possible, please also provide link to the network or use-case where this op is getting used.

As Ops are requested we will add " *To Triage*" pool. If we have 3+ requests for an operation and given its complexity/need the operation will be moved "*To be implemented*" pool. If you want to work on adding support for such op, feel free to comment below to get assigned one. Please avoid pickup up an op that is already being worked on tracked in "*In progress*" pool. 

[Link to the wiki for details](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/wiki/MPS-Backend) on how to add these ops and example PRs.

[**MPS operators coverage matrix**](https://qqaatw.github.io/pytorch-mps-ops-coverage/) - The matrix covers most of the supported operators but is not exhaustive. **Please look at the `In vx.x.x` column, if the box is green, it means that the op implementation is included in the latest release; on the other hand, if the box is yellow, it means the op implementation is in the nightly and has not yet included in the latest release.** Before you comment below, please take a look at this matrix to make sure the operator you're requesting has not been implemented in nightly.  More details can be found on the [readme](https://github.com/qqaatw/pytorch-mps-ops-coverage).

cc @kulinseth @malfet @DenisVieriu97 @jhavukainen

issues.title: [Inductor] Add segment_reduce backward lowering
issues.body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.15.0) (oldest at bottom):
* __->__ #203994
* #203486
* #203455
* #203423

## Linked issue or supporting maintainer

## BC-breaking?

No

## Summary (human written only)

Add `segment_reduce` backward lowering.

## Agent details

> Authored with an AI assistant (Metamate). The human author reviews it before it leaves draft.

This is the fifth PR in the jagged IR stack. `aten._segment_reduce_backward` was a `make_fallback`, so a compiled training step ran the ATen backward kernel even though the forward lowers to a jagged reduction. This PR replaces the fallback with a decomposition into ops that Inductor already lowers.

Each element p of segment s gets the gradient that the ATen kernels give it:

| reduce | gradient of data[p] |
|---|---|
| sum | grad[s] |
| mean | grad[s] / length[s] |
| max, min | 0 unless data[p] is nan or equals out[s] (a tie); then grad[s], divided by the number of ties in s if grad[s] > 0 |
| prod | grad[s] * out[s] / data[p]; where data[p] is 0 or nan, grad[s] * initial * (product of the other elements of s) |

The segment of each element is `searchsorted(offsets, p, right=True) - 1`, one pointwise kernel with `bucketize_binary_search`, and `grad[s]` is then an indirect load: the sum backward is two pointwise kernels. The tie counts for max and min, and for prod the product of the elements that are neither 0 nor nan and the counts of 0 and nan elements, are `segment_reduce` calls, which lower to jagged reductions. Eager computes the prod gradient of a 0 or nan element with a loop over the rest of the segment; these counts give the same value without the loop. Eager divides only positive gradients among ties (#201633), and the decomposition does the same so that compiled and eager agree. Elements that the offsets do not cover get 0, as in eager. On CPU, the `segment_reduce` calls fall back to ATen and the compiled backward still matches eager.

A dedicated lowering would generate the same code, because Inductor already lowers `searchsorted` to a binary search, `gather` to an indirect load and `segment_reduce` to the jagged loop. The decomposition is shorter and keeps working wherever the forward falls back.

### Performance

Backward of `segment_reduce` with default `torch.compile` vs eager on one H100, with the inputs of the forward table in #203455: `offsets` input, average segment length 128 (uniform in [0, 256], or lognormal with sigma 1.5). prod uses data near 1 so that the products stay finite. The backward alone and forward + backward are each captured in a CUDA graph, and the replay is timed with `triton.testing.do_bench`, so the times exclude CPU overhead. Times are in microseconds. Every compiled gradient matches an fp64 reference.

Eager's CUDA backward kernel runs one thread per output element, and that thread loops over its segment, so a long segment dominates the time. The compiled sum backward is a gather whose cost does not depend on the segment lengths, and the counts and products that max and prod need are jagged reductions, which read a segment R0_BLOCK elements at a time. For max and min, the partitioner computes the tie mask in the forward and saves it, so the compiled forward is slower than eager for large inputs (521 to 1138 us for B = 8192, uniform lengths, D = 256, fp32), and the forward + backward speedup is lower than the backward speedup.

## Test plan

The new test compiles the backward of `torch.segment_reduce` for each reduction and compares it with eager on CUDA. Its inputs extend those of `test_simple_1d` in `test/test_segment_reductions.py` (a nan, an empty segment, tied maxima) with tied minima, two zeros for prod and a negative gradient for the tied segment, and it checks that the wrapper does not call `aten._segment_reduce_backward`. The OpInfo tests in `test_torchinductor_opinfo.py` compare the compiled backward with eager for `lengths` and `offsets`, along `axis=1` of 2-D and 3-D inputs, with lengths that do not cover every row, and with `initial`.

```
python test/inductor/test_jagged_ir.py -v
python -m pytest -q test/inductor/test_torchinductor_opinfo.py -k segment_reduce
python test/inductor/test_op_completeness.py
lintrunner -a torch/_inductor/decomposition.py torch/_inductor/lowering.py test/inductor/test_jagged_ir.py
```

issues.title: [Inductor] Lower segment_reduce forward to a jagged reduction
issues.body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.15.0) (oldest at bottom):
* #203994
* #203486
* __->__ #203455
* #203423
* #203415

## Linked issue or supporting maintainer

TODO(nullplay)

## BC-breaking?

No

## Summary (human written only)

Add `segment_reduce` forward lowering with the jagged IR.

## Agent details

> Authored with an AI assistant (Metamate). The human author reviews it before it leaves draft.

This is the third PR in the jagged IR stack. It lowers the forward of `aten.segment_reduce` to a jagged reduction instead of the ATen fallback:

```
out[*o, s, *i] = reduce(data[*o, p, *i] for p in range(start[*o, s], end[*o, s]))
```

There is a single path, based on offsets: the bound is `offsets[s + 1] - offsets[s]` and the start is `offsets[s]`. When only `lengths` is given, the offsets are `cumsum` of the lengths with a leading 0 padded in first. The scan inlines the pad, so the lengths path runs as two kernels: one scan for the offsets and one jagged reduction. The offsets are realized, and the bound reads them with a load even when they are computed only from constants; otherwise Inductor would inline them into the bound. Calls that pass the same offsets or lengths buffer reuse the same offsets and `JaggedRange`. `GraphLowering.jagged_offsets` records them, keyed by kind and buffer name; views get a fresh range. As a result, `sum` and `max` over the same offsets fuse into one kernel, and the lengths scan runs once. `mean` divides the sum by the length in a pointwise epilogue. Empty segments give the same values as eager: 0 for sum, -inf for max, inf for min, 1 for prod, and nan for mean.

`initial` is lowered for `max` and `min` with any value: a pointwise epilogue computes `max(x, initial)` (or `min`), which equals eager seeding the accumulator with `initial`, and an empty segment gives `initial`. `sum`, `mean` and `prod` lower only their identity (0, 0 and 1). With `initial=0`, `mean` gives 0 for an empty segment instead of nan, so the epilogue divides by `max(length, 1)`. Eager adds any other `initial` to the accumulator first, in the data dtype, so those calls fall back.

`lengths` without `unsafe=True` is lowered too. Eager checks on the host that no length is negative and that each row of lengths sums to `data.size(axis)`. The lowering reduces each check to one flag on the device with `any` and asserts on it with `tl.device_assert` and eager's message, so there is no sync. Like `torch._assert_async`, the assert fires asynchronously. This path runs as four kernels: scan, two checks and the reduction. `amax` and `amin`, which PyG passes, lower as `max` and `min`, as in eager.

The lowering keeps the ATen fallback for:
- `lengths` and `offsets` together, because meta and eager disagree on which one wins.
- `indices`, and an `initial` other than the identity for `sum`, `mean` and `prod`.
- Non-Triton devices and the C++/FX wrappers, which cannot pass the jagged numel argument.

fp16 and bf16 data accumulate in fp32, like other Inductor reductions. Eager accumulates in the data dtype, so for long segments the compiled result is closer to an fp64 reference than eager is. `_segment_reduce_backward` stays a fallback. `meta_segment_reduce` now canonicalizes `axis`. Before, a negative `axis` gave the wrong output shape, and the compiled result was silently wrong. Integer data still falls back, because eager supports only floating types.

### Performance

`sum` with default `torch.compile` vs eager on one H100, `offsets` input, average segment length 128 (uniform in [0, 256], or lognormal with sigma 1.5), measured with `triton.testing.do_bench`. Every compiled result matches an fp64 reference. Times are in microseconds; this includes the flat tiling from the previous PR.

| B | lengths (max) | D | dtype | eager | compiled | speedup |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 256 | uniform (256) | 1 | bfloat16 | 7.4 | 5.6 | 1.34x |
| 256 | uniform (256) | 1 | float32 | 7.3 | 5.1 | 1.44x |
| 256 | uniform (256) | 32 | bfloat16 | 37.0 | 9.0 | 4.10x |
| 256 | uniform (256) | 32 | float32 | 36.4 | 10.5 | 3.48x |
| 256 | uniform (256) | 256 | bfloat16 | 45.2 | 18.6 | 2.42x |
| 256 | uniform (256) | 256 | float32 | 50.7 | 25.3 | 2.01x |
| 256 | lognormal (2335) | 1 | bfloat16 | 8.1 | 5.6 | 1.45x |
| 256 | lognormal (2335) | 1 | float32 | 8.0 | 5.6 | 1.43x |
| 256 | lognormal (2335) | 32 | bfloat16 | 264.1 | 12.8 | 20.69x |
| 256 | lognormal (2335) | 32 | float32 | 240.0 | 13.5 | 17.83x |
| 256 | lognormal (2335) | 256 | bfloat16 | 286.9 | 32.7 | 8.76x |
| 256 | lognormal (2335) | 256 | float32 | 280.5 | 39.4 | 7.11x |
| 8192 | uniform (256) | 1 | bfloat16 | 21.4 | 8.0 | 2.66x |
| 8192 | uniform (256) | 1 | float32 | 14.9 | 7.7 | 1.95x |
| 8192 | uniform (256) | 32 | bfloat16 | 69.2 | 50.9 | 1.36x |
| 8192 | uniform (256) | 32 | float32 | 93.2 | 76.3 | 1.22x |
| 8192 | uniform (256) | 256 | bfloat16 | 298.2 | 308.3 | 0.97x |

| 8192 | lognormal (13938) | 1 | bfloat16 | 22.6 | 27.9 | 0.81x |
| 8192 | lognormal (13938) | 1 | float32 | 15.7 | 27.4 | 0.57x |
| 8192 | lognormal (13938) | 32 | bfloat16 | 1526.7 | 166.9 | 9.15x |

Compiled is slower for D = 1 with very long segments (B = 8192, lognormal): eager uses CUB's segmented reduce, and the jagged loop has no split reduction yet.

## Test plan

The new tests compile `torch.segment_reduce` and compare it with eager on CUDA. They cover all five reductions with offsets on 1-D and 2-D data, an inner `axis` with int32 offsets, `lengths` with `unsafe=True` and `unsafe=False` (both lowered; `unsafe=False` emits the device asserts), `amax` and `amin`, and `axis=-2` with offsets, lengths and unsafe lengths. For `initial`, they cover `lengths` with `unsafe=True` and each reduction: `max` with 0 and -inf and `min` with 0.5 are lowered, as are `sum` and `mean` with 0 and `prod` with 1, while `sum` with 1.0 and `prod` with 2.0 fall back. Offsets computed only from constants inside the graph are also lowered. fp16 and bf16 sums are compared with an fp64 reference. The tests also check kernel launch counts: 1 for two reductions on the same offsets, 2 for the same lengths (scan + reduction), and 2 for different offsets. For vertical fusion, a pointwise prologue or epilogue fuses into the jagged reduction (1 launch). A stored prologue, or an epilogue that reduces across segments, stays separate (2 launches). The inputs include an empty segment and a segment longer than one reduction block.

```
python -m pytest -q test/inductor/test_torchinductor_opinfo.py -k segment_reduce
```

issues.title: [MPS] Add native segment_reduce forward pass
issues.body:
## Summary
 
Adds native Metal forward implementations of `segment_reduce` for `sum`, `mean`, `min`, `max` and `prod`, using FP32/FP16/BF16 data and INT32/INT64 lengths or offsets. It reuses the existing ATen frontend and **two forward dispatch stubs**. 
Backward and indices-based reduction remain unsupported. No MPS-only offsets validation is added.



Tracking Issue : https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/141287

## Implementation

The general path assigns one thread per output; long contiguous segments use a threadgroup reduction. Sum/product policies share identity, combine, SIMD and threadgroup operations with ordinary Metal reductions while preserving their load/finalize behavior. Existing min/max policies are reused, and reduction-name conversion is shared in `ReductionType.h`.

The 256-thread launch and scratch capacity derive from shared constants with compile-time constraints. Checked host-side initial-value conversion preserves dtype rounding and scalar overflow errors; redundant shader casts were removed.

Forward OpInfo coverage remains enabled. Missing backward behavior is marked expected-failure, including gradient checks, eager variant consistency, noncontiguous samples and dtype checks. Both lengths and offsets have the additional expectations published in `d512c19305f`. The focused BF16 test has ten cases: five reductions across parallel-contiguous and serial-strided layouts, including noncontiguous inputs, a skipped prefix, empty and long segments.

## Preliminary performance

On an Apple M4 Pro, an FP32 sum over 65,536 values in 16 equal segments took approximately 323 us with the serial shader and 9.7 us with the parallel shader. 

 ## Benchmark

Native product `segment_reduce` on **Apple M4 Pro**, macOS 26.7, with **10 configured CPU threads**.

 ### Queued throughput across shapes and segment counts


| Input shape | Segments | Dtype | Queued CPU | Queued MPS | Speedup | Synchronized CPU | Synchronized MPS | Speedup |
|---|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 262,144 | 64 | FP32 | 197.92 | 46.32 | 4.27x | 202.06 | 161.15 | 1.25x |
| 262,144 | 64 | FP16 | 200.17 | 46.32 | 4.32x | 197.13 | 174.02 | 1.13x |
| 262,144 | 64 | BF16 | 1,121.06 | 48.41 | 23.16x | 1,125.25 | 231.52 | 4.86x |
| 1,048,576 | 16 | FP32 | 810.03 | 195.25 | 4.15x | 800.88 | 360.92 | 2.22x |
| 1,048,576 | 16 | FP16 | 804.55 | 193.47 | 4.16x | 801.86 | 359.45 | 2.23x |
| 1,048,576 | 16 | BF16 | 4,511.18 | 202.47 | 22.28x | 4,479.74 | 383.40 | 11.68x |
| 1,048,576 | 256 | FP32 | 790.69 | 94.49 | 8.37x | 789.48 | 217.05 | 3.64x |
| 1,048,576 | 256 | FP16 | 788.61 | 90.05 | 8.76x | 788.61 | 228.25 | 3.46x |
| 1,048,576 | 256 | BF16 | 4,507.81 | 114.73 | 39.29x | 4,482.26 | 241.94 | 18.53x |
| 4,194,304 | 1,024 | FP32 | 3,181.23 | 250.82 | 12.68x | 3,163.23 | 419.89 | 7.53x |
| 4,194,304 | 1,024 | FP16 | 3,154.13 | 246.90 | 12.77x | 3,152.25 | 426.73 | 7.39x |
| 4,194,304 | 1,024 | BF16 | 17,963.24 | 77.17 | 232.78x | 17,916.33 | 459.62 | 38.98x |
| 8,192 x 128 | 32 | FP32 | 545.95 | 136.92 | 3.99x | 545.64 | 254.28 | 2.15x |
| 8,192 x 128 | 32 | FP16 | 533.61 | 274.62 | 1.94x | 528.25 | 230.58 | 2.29x |
| 8,192 x 128 | 32 | BF16 | 4,105.75 | 277.30 | 14.81x | 4,122.99 | 361.03 | 11.42x |

Segments are equal-length along axis 0. For the 2D input, each segment spans 256 rows with 128 inner values, exercising the serial strided path rather than the contiguous 1D parallel path. Product inputs use adjacent `(0.5, 2)` pairs in randomized order to avoid overflow and underflow. CPU and MPS outputs were exact against the FP64 reference for these controlled product inputs.

### All forward reductions and data types

Each speedup below is the median of the five per-configuration CPU/MPS ratios for the shapes and segment counts above, not a ratio of aggregate times.

| Dtype | Reduction | Queued speedup | Synchronized speedup | MPS wins, synchronized |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| FP32 | sum | 2.78x | 1.76x | 4/5 |
| FP32 | mean | 3.83x | 2.20x | 4/5 |
| FP32 | min | 7.03x | 3.67x | 5/5 |
| FP32 | max | 7.34x | 3.77x | 5/5 |
| FP32 | prod | 4.27x | 2.22x | 5/5 |
| FP16 | sum | 5.62x | 1.88x | 4/5 |
| FP16 | mean | 6.27x | 1.36x | 4/5 |
| FP16 | min | 32.46x | 8.34x | 5/5 |
| FP16 | max | 18.33x | 8.77x | 5/5 |
| FP16 | prod | 4.32x | 2.29x | 5/5 |
| BF16 | sum | 38.94x | 10.57x | 5/5 |
| BF16 | mean | 42.22x | 9.76x | 5/5 |
| BF16 | min | 18.41x | 11.01x | 5/5 |
| BF16 | max | 19.92x | 8.87x | 5/5 |
| BF16 | prod | 23.16x | 11.68x | 5/5 |

Across all reductions and dtypes, MPS was faster in 75/75 queued comparisons and 71/75 synchronized comparisons. All four slower cases used 262,144 elements and 64 segments:

| Reduction | Dtype | Synchronized CPU (us) | Synchronized MPS (us) |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| sum | FP32 | 123.03 | 159.00 |
| sum | FP16 | 127.70 | 203.14 |
| mean | FP32 | 122.60 | 165.40 |
| mean | FP16 | 124.40 | 169.55 |

**Numerical limitations:** sum/mean/min/max use seeded uniform inputs in `[-0.5, 0.5]`. CPU and MPS are checked independently against FP64, with `(rtol, atol)` of FP32 `(1.3e-6, 1e-5)`, FP16 `(1e-3, 1e-5)`, and BF16 `(1.6e-2, 1e-5)`. One MPS FP32 sum case, with 1,048,576 elements and 16 segments, exceeded tolerance: the mismatching output was `16.02954102` versus reference `16.02950263`; CPU produced `16.02973175`. All other MPS configurations passed. CPU sum exceeded tolerance in 14/15 configurations and CPU mean in 10/15. These discrepancies are retained, not hidden by relaxed tolerances.

issues.title: Pipelined dot-input load appears before gdc_wait and produces incorrect results with PDL
issues.body:
### Describe the bug

With Triton 3.7.1 on an H20 (SM90), a consumer kernel using `num_stages=2` produces incorrect results when `tl.extra.cuda.gdc_wait()` is inside its K loop, immediately before the dependent input load.

The generated TTGIR contains an asynchronous copy of the dependent input in the loop prologue, before the GDC wait inside the loop. Disabling PDL, using `num_stages=1`, or adding a GDC wait before the loop makes this standalone reproducer pass.

Is a GDC wait inside a software-pipelined loop expected to prevent this load from being scheduled before the wait? If this placement is unsupported, could you clarify the required pattern? Based on the documented semantics, I expected the dependent load to remain after the wait.

### Environment details

- GPU: NVIDIA H20-3e, compute capability 9.0
- NVIDIA driver: 580.105.08
- Triton: 3.7.1
- PyTorch: 2.13.0+cu132
- `torch.version.cuda`: 13.2
- Python: 3.12.14
- OS: Linux 5.10.134-16.3.al8.x86_64, x86_64
- Tested with the installed versions above; not yet tested against Triton main/nightly.

## Reproducer

Both kernels launch one CTA. The producer signals its dependent, briefly sleeps, and writes ones to X. The store depends on the inline-assembly result to keep it after the delay. The delay widens the overlap window; reproducibility on other devices is not guaranteed by the sleep duration.

Before each pair, X is reset to zero. The producer is launched with `launch_pdl=False` so this reset keeps its normal stream dependency. Only the consumer enables PDL. W is always one, so all output values must be exactly 64.

K is a runtime parameter so the K loop remains available for software pipelining. The source order inside that loop is:

```python
w = tl.load(wp)               # independent weights
tl.extra.cuda.gdc_wait()
x = tl.load(xp).to(tl.bfloat16)  # dependent producer output
acc += tl.dot(x, w)
```

Save the following as `repro_gdc_pipeline.py` and run:

```bash
python repro_gdc_pipeline.py
```

On the affected setup it prints all four controls, then exits with an AssertionError. It also writes TTGIR and PTX for every variant into `repro_gdc_asm/`.

```python
"""Standalone reproducer for GDC wait + software-pipelined dot input loads.

Requires an NVIDIA SM90+ GPU, PyTorch and Triton. No vLLM dependency.
Run: python repro_gdc_pipeline.py
"""
from pathlib import Path

import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


@triton.jit
def producer(X, SIZE: tl.constexpr):
    tl.extra.cuda.gdc_launch_dependents()
    # Keep the producer alive after signaling. The store depends on the asm
    # result, so it cannot move before the delay.
    value = tl.inline_asm_elementwise(
        "nanosleep.u32 1000000; mov.u32 $0, 1;",
        constraints="=r", args=[], dtype=tl.int32, is_pure=False, pack=1,
    )
    i = tl.arange(0, SIZE)
    tl.store(X + i, value.to(tl.float32))


@triton.jit
def consumer(X, W, Y, K, N: tl.constexpr, WAIT_OUTSIDE: tl.constexpr):
    m = tl.arange(0, 64)
    n = tl.program_id(0) * 128 + tl.arange(0, 128)
    k = tl.arange(0, 32)
    xp = X + m[:, None] * K + k[None, :]
    wp = W + k[:, None] * N + n[None, :]
    acc = tl.zeros((64, 128), tl.float32)
    if WAIT_OUTSIDE:
        tl.extra.cuda.gdc_wait()
    for _ in range(tl.cdiv(K, 32)):
        w = tl.load(wp)
        tl.extra.cuda.gdc_wait()
        x = tl.load(xp).to(tl.bfloat16)
        acc += tl.dot(x, w)
        xp += 32
        wp += 32 * N
    tl.store(Y + m[:, None] * N + n[None, :], acc)


def run_case(pdl, stages, outside=False):
    M, N, K = 64, 128, 64
    x = torch.zeros((M, K), device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32)
    w = torch.ones((K, N), device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
    y = torch.empty((M, N), device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32)

    def launch():
        x.zero_()
        # Normal producer launch preserves the dependency on x.zero_().
        producer[(1,)](x, M * K, num_warps=4, launch_pdl=False)
        return consumer[(N // 128,)](
            x, w, y, K, N, outside,
            num_warps=4, num_stages=stages, launch_pdl=pdl,
        )

    kernel = launch()
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    stem = f"pdl{int(pdl)}_stages{stages}_outside{int(outside)}"
    output = Path(__file__).with_name("repro_gdc_asm")
    output.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    for ext in ("ttgir", "ptx"):
        (output / f"{stem}.{ext}").write_text(kernel.asm[ext])

    graph = torch.cuda.CUDAGraph()
    with torch.cuda.graph(graph):
        launch()
    failures = 0
    worst = 0.0
    for _ in range(20):
        graph.replay()
        torch.cuda.synchronize()
        # All inputs are one after the producer: every output must equal K.
        error = (y - K).abs().max().item()
        failures += int(not torch.equal(y, torch.full_like(y, K)))
        worst = max(worst, error)
    print(f"{stem}: failed_replays={failures}/20 max_abs_error={worst}", flush=True)
    return failures


def main():
    print(f"torch={torch.__version__}, CUDA={torch.version.cuda}, "
          f"triton={triton.__version__}", flush=True)
    print(f"GPU={torch.cuda.get_device_name()}, "
          f"capability={torch.cuda.get_device_capability()}", flush=True)
    assert torch.cuda.get_device_capability()[0] >= 9, "Requires SM90+"
    assert run_case(False, 2) == 0, "Non-PDL control failed"
    assert run_case(True, 1) == 0, "Single-stage control failed"
    failures = run_case(True, 2)
    assert run_case(True, 2, outside=True) == 0, "Outside-wait control failed"
    assert failures == 0, (
        "Dependent loads appear to cross gdc_wait with num_stages=2: "
        f"{failures}/20 graph replays produced incorrect results"
    )


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

## Actual result

```text
torch=2.13.0+cu132, CUDA=13.2, triton=3.7.1
GPU=NVIDIA H20-3e, capability=(9, 0)
pdl0_stages2_outside0: failed_replays=0/20 max_abs_error=0.0
pdl1_stages1_outside0: failed_replays=0/20 max_abs_error=0.0
pdl1_stages2_outside0: failed_replays=20/20 max_abs_error=32.0
pdl1_stages2_outside1: failed_replays=0/20 max_abs_error=0.0
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/linitra24/vllm_my/tmp/lora_pdl/repro_gdc_pipeline.py", line 102, in <module>
    main()
  File "/home/linitra24/vllm_my/tmp/lora_pdl/repro_gdc_pipeline.py", line 95, in main
    assert failures == 0, (
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^
AssertionError: Dependent loads appear to cross gdc_wait with num_stages=2: 20/20 graph replays produced incorrect results
```

The outside-wait control adds one wait before the loop and leaves the original in-loop wait in place.

Expected: all four variants produce exactly 64 in every output element.

## Generated-code evidence

In `pdl1_stages2_outside0.ttgir`, `%xp_22` is derived from the producer output pointer `%X`. Its asynchronous copy appears at line 72, before the `scf.for` at line 74. The GDC wait is inside the loop at line 85.

Abbreviated for readability:

```text
%xp_16 = tt.splat %X ...
...
%x_38 = ttg.async_copy_global_to_local %xp_22, %x_36 ...
...
%acc_40:8 = scf.for ... {
    ...
    %9 = tt.elementwise_inline_asm "griddepcontrol.wait; // dummy $0"
         {constraints = "=r", packed_element = 1 : i32, pure = false} -> i32
    ...
}
```

The PTX likewise contains dependent-input `cp.async.cg.shared.global` instructions at lines 123–135, before the `griddepcontrol.wait` at line 323. Full TTGIR, PTX and the execution log are attached.

This suggests the asynchronous input copy is moved ahead of the synchronization during software pipelining. I have not identified the responsible compiler pass or verified a compiler fix.

For this reproducer, both `num_stages=1` and an additional wait before the loop avoid the incorrect results.

Reference: [Triton GDC wait documentation](https://triton-lang.org/main/python-api/generated/triton.language.extra.cuda.gdc_wait.html).

issues.title: [Gluon] Prototype CTA specialization
issues.body:
## Summary

Prototype `gl.cta_specialize(functions_and_args, partition_num_ctas)` so a Gluon program can divide its current CTAs into independently programmed subgroups. Each subgroup has its own `num_ctas()`, layouts, CTA ranks, and barriers. Splits can nest, and the parent CTAs synchronize before the split and after all regions finish.

Parent shared-memory allocations can be passed into regions using ordinary `smem.slice(...)` views. The compiler checks that a view belongs to exactly the receiving CTA range and rebases its layout while preserving the allocation, strides, and local offsets. Writes are visible through the parent descriptor after the join.

```python
# With four CTAs and a shared layout that places these halves on CTAs 0–1 and 2–3:
gl.cta_specialize([
    (worker_a, (smem.slice(0, 16),)),
    (worker_b, (smem.slice(16, 16),)),
], [2, 2])
```

## Prototype limits

- NVIDIA Hopper or newer; partition counts are positive powers of two and sum to the current CTA count.
- Inline functions and synchronous operations only. Warp specialization, asynchronous cluster operations, and sanitizer instrumentation are not supported within CTA-specialized regions.
- Regions return no runtime values. Distributed tensors and tensor-memory descriptors cannot be captured; shared-memory captures require statically provable CTA ownership and an unpartitioned shared layout.

## Validation

Built on an isolated GB300 devbox and verified matching source hashes. Only formatting changed afterward; Python ASTs and normalized C++ token streams were checked unchanged:

- 14 compiler/frontend tests passed, including invalid partition counts, nested contexts, unsupported operations, and invalid shared-memory captures.
- 16 GPU tests passed: 8 shared-memory capture cases and 8 existing CTA specialization cases. Coverage includes nested and uneven splits, nonzero slice offsets, padded/swizzled/linear shared layouts, runtime buffer indices, parent reads after joining, and subgroup synchronization.
- 5 focused lit tests passed for IR validation, NVIDIA lowering, cluster-barrier allocation, and warp-group allocation/lowering.
- Local Python syntax, diff-whitespace, and pre-commit checks passed.

issues.title: [TUTORIALS] Avoid per-case streams in fused-softmax benchmark
issues.body:
Fixes #11661

The fused-softmax tutorial created and selected a new PyTorch device stream in every `benchmark()` call. This made each case use a different stream while the caching allocator retained memory from earlier cases, causing reserved memory to grow through the sweep.

Remove the two per-case stream calls so the benchmark uses the current stream. On an 8 GiB RTX 2000 Ada running Windows, the full 294-case sweep completed with this change alone. Reserved memory still grew (to 23,016 MiB under WDDM), so this does not establish that the original 6 GiB OOM is fixed on that card.

issues.title: [GSan][IR] Make GDC ops IR nodes, and support PDL in GSan
issues.body:
This changes how GSan models stream synchronization. Each stream maintains a ring buffer of three vector clocks, and each kernel receives a monotonically increasing `kernel_id`.

- At kernel completion, each CTA publishes its vector clock using an atomic max on `stream_clock[kernel_id % 3]`.
- For a normal launch, the kernel initializes its clock from `stream_clock[(kernel_id - 1) % 3]`, acquiring the previous kernel’s aggregated clock.
- For a PDL launch, the kernel initializes from `stream_clock[(kernel_id - 2) % 3]`, acquiring the kernel from two launches ago.
- When a PDL kernel executes `gdc_wait`, it acquires `stream_clock[(kernel_id - 1) % 3]`, synchronizing with its immediate predecessor.

This also completely removes the need for the separate `synchronize_launch_stream` function.
